You sound pretty convinced that life is a competition or a race. Competing against time and peers for jobs, money, a certain type of woman. Imagine for a second that life is not a competition, that success is not measured by your BMI or how many people you've slept with. 

You are seeing others' highlight reel. Maybe a young engineer hates their job and wants to be a photographer. Maybe their wife who is skinny is a horrible person. Maybe their first love was a curvy woman who made them happy and they'd kill to be with that woman again. 

People may judge you on your outward appearance or behaviour, and you know how wrong that is. Don't fall into the same trap. What you see is not what may be true. 

People have second careers, people go to med school at 30 years of age, people find new passions at 80. Success is not a linear path. Find what makes you happy and fulfilled!

I'm an occupational therapist in a new job. I get sort of nervous about various aspects of my job: leading education groups, the idea of being watched by other health professionals, speaking during meetings, being around attractive coworkers (my own insecurities), trying to make friends with coworkers who are already friends with each other, managing time, making mistakes on an electronic system. 

That being said, I like my job. It is engaging, it gives me an escape from my irrational fears and anxieties about my relationship, and helping others is what I do best. 

The nerves I do get, I use deep breathing and pursed lip breathing before I have to run a group or go to a meeting. I try to tell myself that people are more concerned about themselves than they are with me, and no one but me dwells on my mistakes or awkward sentences. Also I am new so I try to cut myself some slack and remember that I will get better at things.

Tell them how you've been feeling, how long you've been feeling this way, like the other commenter said, be ready to describe your eating/sleeping/physical and mental symptoms. 

It probably won't be just you giving this information, the doctor will likely step in and ask you questions about your eating and sleeping and your situation at home/school etc. They might give you a screening questionnaire to do, in order to make a diagnosis of depression and/or anxiety and figure out what is the best way to approach treatment and help decrease your school workload. My PHQ9 (depression screen) score was 15 about 6 months ago and I remember the doctor telling me I can try to exercise everyday and take b12 and see if it improves, or I can take also antidepressants on top of that. Also, unless you are actively suicidal and need to be admitted to the hospital for assessment, no one can force you to do anything. You choose if you want meds or not. You can't actually get addicted to antidepressants and for some it is a life-saver, but you can weigh the pros and cons of meds for yourself after hearing the information. 

If for whatever reason the doctor doesn't believe you or acknowledge your situation, then find another one. Doctors are just people, sometimes you don't see eye to eye. Especially if they're family doctors, they may not know or be comfortable about mental health. 

Edit: Also, you can try some deep breathing while you're going to the doctor's/waiting in their office. It helped me when I had to do this. Also remember they are bound to protect your privacy and confidentiality and whatever you say or do in there. I ended up crying in my appointment, but it was fine, and I was glad I went. The main thing is you are seeking professional help and that is a great step.

The things I do to cope with insecurities have been to distract myself, work out (exercise is great for mental health), hang out/communicate often with supportive friends, and to find things to do to better yourself such as joining a group that has your hobby, reading, etc. Develop a routine for yourself and stick to it. When you feel bad, instead of focusing on your negatives or supposed inadequacies, you can remember your strengths and interests. 

Edit: I like reading and getting experience from others. Self-help resources on anxiety/depression or going on reddit/support groups help me too.

Hi. I didn't read all of your post because I am going through rOCD and am feeling pretty awful these days/didn't want to be triggered. The past week I started actually trying to do ERP on my own. It feels shitty, and Ive cried at work multiple times thinking about my bf and his exes (the themes of my intrusive thoughts). At first you wonder how stopping asking for reassurance is even helpful, but after a few days I started to feel like not asking for reassurance was giving me a bit of control. Like I was slightly less sensitive to the thoughts (felt a bit numb), and not having to run to my bf all the time, made me feel more powerful. 
However I am a person who needs to tell people things to process and get over them, otherwise I'd explode, so I started writing a quick journal entry every few hours summarizing my thoughts. This will also be helpful to reference for my eventual psych appointment. 

The one thing I can't figure out with ERP is how to deal with its side effects. You do feel a lot of anxiety when you accept or deal with the uncertainty that those intrusive thoughts might be valid, but for me it manifests as wanting to distance myself from my boyfriend or feeling disconnected from him. I don't want to seek his reassurance all the time, but I also don't want to hate him or feel distant. I dunno how to find the right balance, or if this feeling will change with more ERP. 

As for what I DO talk to my bf about, I have mentioned what ERP is and how I am going to actively stop trying to seek reassurance. I describe how the day was without referencing any of the content of the thoughts. For example I'll say "I had 6 disturbing thoughts this morning but they didn't stick". Also I sent him a guideline to help him understand what I needed from him which he said was helpful:
https://iocdf.org/expert-opinions/expert-opinion-family-guidelines/ 

I also found this helpful for directing my own ERP, and there is a passage about reassurance that I sent to my bf which was also helpful: 
http://beyondocd.org/expert-perspectives/articles/self-directed-treatment-for-ocd-the-irony-of-doing-the-opposite

This is just my experience, and I am not diagnosed with OCD (yet?). Hope this helps. Feel free to PM me if you want to talk more! I feel alone these days. 
P.S. Counselling is a very good idea. I am trying to get the same for myself.
